transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?
Hello doctor, thank you for seeing me. Lately I keep forgetting everyday things I’m supposed to do, like taking my pills or bringing what I need to church events, even when I write them down.

Have you also been feeling very depressed, or had times when you felt unusually energetic or needed much less sleep than usual? Have you had any experiences like hearing or seeing things others don’t, or strongly believing something others say isn’t true?

No, I haven't felt depressed or unusually energetic with less sleep, and I certainly haven't experienced any unusual sights, sounds, or beliefs. My mood has been generally fine, it's really just these daily mix-ups and forgetfulness that are frustrating me.
Because of your memory problems, are you still able to manage everyday activities like paying bills, cooking, shopping, and taking your medicines on your own, or do you now need help with these?

I still try to manage everything on my own, but I regularly forget routine things like taking my vitamins and pills, even with phone alarms and lists. I'm not completely dependent, but my daughter has started double-checking my plans and schedules because she's worried I'll drop the ball.

Aside from reminders from your daughter, do these memory problems make you unable to handle important daily tasks by yourself, like paying bills, managing medications, cooking safely, or getting to familiar places? Or are you still independent but just slower or more forgetful than before?

I am still independent and can handle cooking, driving, and paying bills on my own, but I have become much more forgetful and disorganized. I keep misplacing volunteer sign-up sheets or double-booking events, which has made people at church stop relying on me for important tasks. I don't need help caring for myself, but the forgetfulness is definitely getting in the way of my daily life.

Have you had any medical or brain-related problems around the time this memory trouble started, such as a stroke, head injury, seizures, Parkinson’s disease, thyroid problems, or a new medication? If so, what was it and when did it happen?

No, I haven't experienced any of those medical issues, head injuries, or new medications around the time these difficulties started. My physical health has actually been quite good otherwise, so there wasn't any major change like that.
When did these memory problems first start, and have they been gradually getting worse over time or did they come on suddenly? About how long has this been going on?

This has been going on and steadily getting worse for almost two years now. It was a very gradual change that started after my husband passed away and I retired, which left my days much more unstructured. Since then, keeping track of everything has just become harder and harder.

Because of your memory problems, have you ever gotten lost in a familiar place, left the stove on, missed paying important bills, or taken the wrong medicines in a way that put your safety at risk? Or is it mostly forgetfulness and disorganization without those major problems?

No, fortunately I have never gotten lost or left the stove on, and I haven't had any dangerous medication mix-ups. It is really just everyday forgetfulness and disorganization, like missing my daily vitamins or forgetting to bring my supplies to quilting meetings.

Has anyone close to you, like your daughter or friends at church, clearly noticed that your memory or organization has worsened compared with a couple of years ago? If so, what changes have they pointed out?

Yes, sadly, others have definitely noticed and it has been quite embarrassing. People at church and in my volunteer groups have stopped relying on me for important tasks because of my constant mix-ups, and my daughter now double-checks my plans because she's worried I'll forget the grandkids' schedules.

Have you ever been told by a doctor that your memory problems are due to a medical or brain condition, such as a stroke, Parkinson’s disease, seizures, or another neurological illness? Or has no clear medical cause been found?

No, I've never been diagnosed with any medical or neurological conditions like a stroke or Parkinson's. When I brought up these memory struggles with my primary care doctor, they didn't find a physical cause and recommended this psychiatric evaluation to look into underlying attentional issues instead.

Do you mainly lose track because your mind drifts and you have trouble focusing in the moment, or do you feel you pay attention fine but still cannot remember the information later? Can you give one recent example?

It is definitely more that my mind drifts off and I lose focus in the moment, rather than just forgetting things later. For instance, when I sit down to read the notes from our garden committee or follow a Bible study lesson, my mind will wander after just a few minutes and I'll realize I’ve completely missed half of what I was reading.
Before age 12, did you already have similar problems with attention, distractibility, or disorganization at school, work, or home? Or did these difficulties only begin later in adulthood?

Yes, these difficulties actually go back to when I was a young girl in grade school. My teachers used to write on my report cards that I was bright but "daydreamed too much" and forgot to turn in homework I had already finished. I also talked out of turn so much that they had to move my seat more than once.

Do these attention and organization problems happen in several parts of your life, like at home, in social activities, and in past jobs or school, rather than only since retirement? Can you give one example from adulthood before the last two years?

Yes, they currently affect multiple areas, from forgetting my pills at home to messing up my volunteer and church commitments. However, during my adult working years prior to these last two years, I didn't really struggle because my job had a very rigid, clear structure. Back then, I actually had a reputation for being incredibly organized and reliable, so this is quite new for my adulthood.

Before retirement, even if your job structure helped, did you still need unusual effort, strict routines, or reminders to manage attention and organization in daily life? Or did these problems truly disappear for most of your adult years and only return in the last two years?

I'm not entirely sure, as I haven't really thought about it that way. I think I just did what I had to do to keep up with my work back then, and having a busy, set routine seemed to keep me on track without me realizing it. It didn't feel like an unusual effort at the time.

Outside of your structured job years, did you continue to have lifelong problems with things like losing items, forgetting appointments, procrastinating, or being easily distracted at home or in other settings? Or did those problems truly stop for many years and only start again in the last two years?

Looking back, those tendencies were always there since childhood, but the tight structure of my working years helped me keep them under control and maintain a reliable reputation. It was only after retiring and losing my husband two years ago that the complete lack of structure caused these lifelong struggles to resurface and disrupt my daily life. It feels like they were always under the surface but only became a real problem again once I lost my daily routine.

During your adult years before retirement, did you still often need calendars, lists, strict routines, or other reminders just to stay organized, even if you were functioning well? Or did your attention and organization problems truly go away completely for many years?

I'm not entirely sure, as I haven't really thought about it that way. My previous job as a senior center coordinator had a lot of built-in structure that kept me on track, but I really don't recall having this much trouble back then.

Before retirement, outside of your job itself, were you also relying heavily on planners, sticky notes, strict routines, or help from others to keep track of appointments, chores, or bills at home? Or were you managing those things easily without special systems?

I'm not entirely sure, but I don't recall needing any heavy systems or special planners back then. My daily routine just felt much more automatic and structured when I was working and my husband was alive, which is a big contrast to the struggle I'm facing now.

Compared with your usual lifelong distractibility, do you feel there has been a clear new decline in your thinking or memory over the last two years, even when you are focused? For example, do you now forget conversations, repeat questions, or have trouble learning new information more than you used to?

I don't think I have noticed that kind of memory decline, like forgetting entire conversations or repeating my questions to people. I'm not entirely sure, but it really feels more like a struggle with staying focused in the moment rather than actually losing my memory.

Before the last two years, did these attention problems ever cause clear difficulties in adulthood outside of work, such as missed appointments, unpaid bills, chronic lateness, or relationship problems? If yes, what was one example?

No, before the last two years, I didn't really have those kinds of difficulties in my adult life at all. I actually had a reputation for being very reliable and kept things together well, likely because my life was much more structured when I was working as a senior center coordinator and my husband was still alive. These issues only became a real problem after my retirement and his passing left my schedule completely unstructured.

As a child, besides daydreaming at school, did these attention problems also cause clear trouble at home or with friends, and did they continue in some form through adulthood even before retirement? Or did they fully go away for many years and only reappear in the last two years?

No, I don't recall those childhood issues causing any major trouble at home or with my friends back then. During my adulthood, my structured role as a senior center coordinator and my marriage kept me very reliable, so those tendencies didn't really get in the way. They only became a major, disruptive problem in the last two years after my husband passed and I retired, leaving my days completely unstructured.
Before age 12, did your inattention or distractibility clearly cause problems in at least two settings, like both school and home or with friends? What is one example besides daydreaming in class?

I do remember these issues starting back in grade school, though I mostly recall the problems being at school rather than having clear memories of other settings. For example, I would often completely forget to turn in homework that I had actually finished, and I talked out of turn so much that the teacher had to move my seat.

Before age 12, did your attention problems also clearly cause trouble at home or with friends—not just at school? For example, were you often forgetting chores, losing things, or getting in trouble for not listening at home?

I definitely remember having those issues at school, like daydreaming, forgetting homework, and talking out of turn. But to be honest, I don't clearly recall having major trouble at home or with friends back then, and I'm not really sure about those other settings.

Before age 12, did your attention problems clearly happen in another setting besides school, such as often forgetting chores, losing things, or not listening at home? If yes, what is one specific example?

I'm not really sure, and I don't recall clearly if those problems happened at home or in other settings before age 12. I mostly just remember the issues my teachers pointed out on my report cards at school back then.

Is there anyone who knew you well as a child—like a sibling or old report cards—who could confirm whether these attention problems also happened at home, not just at school? If not, do you remember often forgetting chores, losing things, or getting in trouble for not listening at home before age 12?

Yes, I actually still have my old report cards from grade school before age 12. On them, my teachers wrote that I daydreamed too much, forgot to turn in homework I had actually completed, and talked out of turn so much that they had to move my seat more than once.

Do any of those old report cards, or a family member who knew you then, show that these attention problems also happened at home before age 12, such as forgetting chores, losing things, or not listening? Or were the problems only documented at school?

The report cards only documented the school-related issues, and I don't recall any written notes or family complaints about my chores at home. My teachers very clearly wrote that I was bright but "daydreamed too much," forgot to turn in completed homework, and talked out of turn so much that my seat had to be moved multiple times. So, those school struggles are the only ones definitely documented from back then.

Did your current forgetfulness and disorganization begin as a clear new change after retirement and your husband’s death, or do they feel like the same lifelong attention problems you had as a child becoming more noticeable without structure? Which of those fits better overall?

It definitely feels like the same lifelong attention issues I had as a child, like my daydreaming and forgetting homework, becoming much more noticeable now. Without the structure of my job and my husband here, those old struggles have just become so much harder to manage on my own.

Before age 12, can you remember even one clear example of these attention problems causing trouble at home or with friends, not just at school? For example, often forgetting chores, losing things, or getting in trouble for not listening.

I don't really recall specific examples of having these troubles at home or with friends before age 12. My clearest memories from back then are mostly related to school, like my report cards mentioning my daydreaming and getting my seat moved.

Do you have a parent, sibling, or anyone else who knew you well before age 12 who could confirm that you also had attention problems at home or with friends, not just at school? If yes, what did they notice?

I'm afraid I don't have anyone available who could confirm those details for you now. At my age, there isn't really anyone left who could speak to how I behaved at home as a young child. My parents passed away years ago, and I don't have any siblings or childhood friends who would remember those kinds of daily details.

Before age 12, did your daydreaming or distractibility ever clearly cause problems in another setting besides school, such as forgetting chores, losing things, or getting in trouble at home? If yes, what is one specific example you remember?
I really don't remember any specific examples of these problems causing trouble at home or outside of school before age 12. I'm just not sure if it was an issue in those other settings back then.

Even if you can’t remember childhood details, before the last two years did you ever have a long period in adult life when you were truly free of attention and organization problems without needing structure or reminders? Or have these traits always been there underneath, just kept in check by routine?

Looking back, I believe these traits have always been there underneath, but they were kept in check by the heavy structure of my past life. Having a demanding job as a senior center coordinator and having my husband around provided a natural routine that kept me organized. Once I retired and he passed away, losing that daily structure caused these lifelong tendencies—which go back to my childhood daydreaming—to finally surface and become unmanageable.
Before age 12, can you remember any clear problems from your distractibility in another setting besides school, such as at home, with chores, or with friends? Even one specific example would help.

I really don't recall any specific examples of these issues at home or with friends before age 12. I mostly just remember the feedback from my teachers about my schoolwork and behavior in class, like daydreaming or talking out of turn.
